POSSE TAKES ALLEGED ASSAILANT OF WOMAN
Leesburg Man Run Down Within 40 Minutes After Attempted Attack.
LEESBURG, Va., Aug. 13.—Frank Anderson, colored, was run down and captured yesterday by a posse of 150 citizens led by Sheriff Edwards, within forty minutes after he had made, it is alleged, an attempted attack on Mrs. Arthur Bridler at her home in Belmont Park.

The negro, according to the woman, slipped up behind her as she was shelling peas on her front porch and struck her on the head with a rock. He was frightened off by her cries. The alleged attack took place about 9 o'clock this morning. Anderson has been placed in the Leesburg jail. There was some talk of mob violence.
frank-anderson-leesburg-1920-08-12.A2:
VIRGINIA JAIL
UNDER GUARD
Troops Ready for Call in Loudoun County to Prevent Mob Violence.
(Special to Washington Herald.)

Winchester, Va., Aug. 13.—Local militia is in readiness tonight for a call to defend Winchester jail where Frank Anderson, 25 years old, a Loudoun County negro, is confined under guard in a steel cage after being rushed from Leesburg under heavy guard.

He was arrested at Leesburg yesterday charged with criminal assault on Mrs. Virginia Cridler. 19 years old. Infuriated Loudoun County citizens, it was learned here, stormed the jail at Leesburg all night last night.

Sheriff Edwards with his guards and deputies fought off the mob.

After a hasty conference between Sheriff Edwards and Gov. Westmoreland Davis at his country home at Leesburg it was decided to get the negro over the county line.

Sheriff Pannett, of Frederick County, was requested to receive the prisoner. It is said Anderson's father threatened to blow up the town of Purcellville, where he lives, if any violence is done his son.
frank-anderson-leesburg-1920-08-12.A3:
LOUDOUN CITIZENS STORM COUNTY JAIL FOR NEGRO
Alleged Assailant of Young Bride Brought to Winchester for Safe Keeping. (Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
Safe Keeping.
(Special to The Times-Disp
WINGESTHRU XA

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
WINCHESTER, VA., August 13.—Frank Anderson, a Loudoun County negro, charged with attempting to attack Mrs. Virginia Cridler, 19 years old, a bride of three months, was brought here late today by Sheriff Edwards, of Loudoun, and placed in a steel cage in Winchester jail for safe keeping. The attempted outrage is said to have occurred while Mrs. Cridler, who lives near Goose Creek, was on her way to a store.

Citizens of Loudoun County, it was said, stormed the Loudoun County jail at Leesburg last night demanding that Anderson, who had been apprehended, be turned over to them and lynched. Sheriff Edwards fought off the mob, which apparently lacked a leader, and when he heard lynching talk again this afternoon he conferred with Governor Davis, who was at his Leesburg home, and Sheriff Pannett, of Frederick County, was requested to receive Anderson. The prisoner is heavily guarded.

Local militiamen were ready tonight for any emergency. It is the intention to keep Anderson here until the next term of the Circuit Court of Loudoun County. Beyond denying his guilt, Anderson refused to discuss the affair with Sheriff Pannett.

The prisoner is about twenty-five years old, and inclined to be surly. Sheriff Edwards said the father of Anderson had threatened to blow up the town of Purcellville if his son was prosecuted. The Andersons are regarded as "bad men" in Loudoun County.

OFF THE WIRES
NEW YORK.—Coastwise longshoremen, who have been on strike here since March 12, voted at a mass meeting last night to go back to work Monday morning provided the steamship owners get rid of the strikebreakers they have employed. They agreed to submit their demands, including a wage increase of 15 cents an hour, to arbitration after they return to work.

CONSTANTINOPLE.—Bolsheviki at Odessa seized the French steamers Catavia and Eigrette, which landed Russian prisoners there from France, and refused to release them. The French battleship Edgard Quinet, with three destroyers, was rushed from Constantinople and threatened to raze the city unless the steamers were released, it was learned here.

NEW YORK.—Six hundred birds, beasts and reptiles from Regent park zoological garden, London, arrived here on the steamer Minnesota en route to the Bronx zoo. Rare creatures in the collection included a white wild ass, said to be the only one in captivity; a panda-cat bear, one of the smallest in existence, standing only eighteen inches in height; five black apes with white eyebrows, two wild Indian swans, some black-necked grackles from China, and snakes, including diamond pythons and cobras.

TOLEDO.—Edward Ray, of Great Britain, won the national open golf championship of America at Inverness with a score of 295 for 72 holes, thus carrying the cup to England for the second time. Harry Vardon having won the title twenty years ago and lacking only two strokes of capturing it again yesterday.

WINCHESTER, Va.—Frank Anderson, a negro, accused of an attempted attack on a white woman in Loudoun county, was secretly taken from the jail at Leesburg, Va., last night while a mob intent on lynching him was surrounding it, and brought to Winchester by Sheriff Edwards for safe keeping. Gov. Davis directed the removal, and militiamen at Winchester were ordered to remain in readiness for call if further attempts at lynching appeared.

ATLANTIC CITY, N. J.—As the result of an accident to her machinery two weeks ago the 5,000-ton tanker Texaco, owned by the Texas Oil company, limped into port here under improvised sails. She will be towed to New York. The tanker carries a crew of twenty-six and is bound from Port Arthur.

HOUSTON "ROUGHS" ARE LOOKING FOR TROUBLE
HOUSTON, Tex., August 23.—A number of brutal assaults have been made here recently on Colored street car passengers by car conductors. Following a brutal assault made on Mrs. Gertrudo Ford, a Colored woman, and other was made on a Colored youth, and but for the wrenching of a gun from the hands of the conductor, by a passenger, the boy would have been shot. It is said practically all the conductors on car lines here go armed hoping for an opportunity to shoot down some Colored passenger.

DESOTO, Mo., Aug. 12.—Following a trail of blood, a posse of angry farmers today tracked a negro. Mo. charged with criminally attacking 12-year-old Gertrude Wilson, to a clump of Woods about three miles from here. His capture was expected momentarily and threats of a lynching were made. By United Press LONDON, Aug. 12.—Archbishop Mannix today told the United Press he was determined to visit Ireland in defiance of the British government. By United Press
VINELAND, Mo., Aug. 12.—Three hundred residents of Vineland who have been searching the surrounding country since yesterday afternoon for a negro who attempted to attack a 12-year-old white girl believe they have him surrounded in the woods near town today.

The girl was on her way to the postoffice on horseback. She screamed when the negro stopped her horse, and residents of a near-by farmhouse came to her rescue. The negro fled.

The negro was sighted by members of the posse this morning skulking through the woods. P. M. Polittee, a farmer fired his gun at him. Blood was found near where the negro was seen.

St. Louis authorities were appealed for bloodhounds. The posse, which numbered 300 at the start, was rapidly increasing in number as farmers from all parts of the county joined.

Members of the posse denied that the negro would be lynched if he was caught. They stated, however, that they were determined to bring him to justice.

The negro will be taken to the girl's home for identification. If she identifies him a lynching is feared.

The negro said he was Davis Robinson, 25, of Chicago. Buckshot wounds were found in his head, back and*legs.

the allies that the territorial integrity and true boundaries of Russia shall be respected. as a means of depriving the soviet usurpers of what has heretofore been a rallying cry to the patriotism of Russians little in sympathy with their methods or their purposes.

We do not know that any better policy than this has anywhere been announced. It has at least the advantage that it is a policy, clear, plain, easily understood, not to be misrepresented. It is notice to the world that the United States, in relation to the vital problem of Russia, is not merely drifting. It may suggest the real solution.—New York World (Dem.).

Concerning Russia, after two years of indecision, the administration has last spoken. There is a policy, though only a negative one.

From an idealistic point of view the policy is of course open to criticism. Ethics are not satisfied when we say that the Lenine government will not be recognized because the Russian people have had no part in its creation, and then in the next breath indicate that we will not act to secure to the Russian people the right of democratic self-rule.

But from the practical point of view much can be urged in support of the declaration, and it may be predicted that it will satisfy the country. It frees us from direct complicity in the bolshevist crime against civilization, and at least expresses a moral condemnation. It is worth much to have the president declare: "That the present rulers of Russia do not rule by the will or consent of the Russian people, is an incontestable fact."

Moreover, Russia is large and amorphous, and it has never been clear how the allies, except with the active assistance of great masses of Russians, could effect a reorganization. Certainly this country has no desire to attempt the job alone.

We have a reapplication and revival of the course pursued toward Huerta. In the new case, as in the old, the usurper will not be received in friendship, "The hand of Douglas is his own." Othedwise, as also the theory was with respect to Mexico, but Russia is further away.—New York Tribune (Rep.).

Cox On Our Foreign Element.

In discussing the foreign element in America he takes sharp issue with Mr. Harding. The republican nominee thinks it important that we should so mould our American policy that these foreigners will be satisfied. He opposes the league because he tells us that where another nation is involved in a controversy the immigrants here from that country could not be expected to feel kindly toward us. Cox says that through education, and bringing these foreigners in on the moulding of public opinion, they must be brought to the point where in any controversy between the land of their birth and this they will be Americans.

Harding looks upon this country as an international boarding house.

Cox considers it a nation.

Perhaps the most interesting phase of his discussion of the foreigner is his indictment of our usual attitude toward him—treating him merely as a labor unit and not as a man. This result in making him migratory; leaves him without a home of his own; results in herding with his kind; discourages the learning of our language, which in turn prevents the reading of our papers and the resulting understanding of our institutions and our point of view. He would change this attitude toward the foreigner.

Meanwhile, as he is learning, he would be tolerant of his misunderstandings.—Fort Wayne Journal-Gazette (Dem.).

The Paramount Issue.

No matter what may be thundered from the political platform as the paramount issue of the campaign, it is certain most listeners would vastly prefer to hear some practical recommendation for reducing the cost of living and lightening the burden of taxation. The belief in the minds of many people is that taxation burdens ought to be growing lighter, now that so many months have passed since the war was ended. It is not at all certain the public, all the millions of people of the nation, will agree to the choice of questions by the candidates, or be ready to accept the recommendations of the platform writers and campaign managers as to what is the real issue.

If some speaker should appear during the campaign with a promising means for reducing living costs, he would make himself and his plan immensely popular, would be in demand everywhere, and the public sentiment he would rouse would definitely make and fix the paramount issue. There is a tremendous feeling in the hearts of people that taxation burdens ought to be lightened and could be without injury to any governmental activity. There is keen disappointment in the hearts of consumers that governmental powers have not availed to protect the public from being plundered by profiteers, who are still squeezing their profits from the public. Thus far not a single definite, rational plan for curing these troubles and righting these conditions has been given the public.

WOUNDED NEGRO HELD Posse Member Drops Dead at End of the 100-mile Chase. By United Press
BLACKWELL, Mo., Aug 14.—A negro alleged to have attempted to attack Gertrude Wilson, aged 12, on a road south of Vineland Wednesday afternoon, was captured at 8 o'clock this morning about a mile north of here. He had been shot and wounded, but reports that he had been killed proved erroneous.

Although posses have been pursuing the negro for three days and the entire countryside has taken part in the manhunt, his captors here say they intend to turn him over to the Jefferson County authorities. Sheriff Frank Clark of Hillsboro has been notified and is on his way here by automobile to place the negro under arrest.

Nearly 100 miles have been covered in the chase, which extended in a semicircular course over three counties only to come to an end about two miles from where it began.

Clyde Nicholson of Ridgewood, aged 22, made the negro prisoner. Nicholson was one of more than a score of men who started from here shortly after dawn to beat the woods north of this city. The members of the
fly after dawn to beat the woods north of this city. The members of the posses separated and Nicholson was alone when he came upon the negro who started to run. Nicholson fired six shots and the negro stopped and gave himself up.

The posse reassembled and brought the prisoner to town. It was found that he had been wounded in the back of the head, the back and in the left arm with buckshot. A physician said his injuries were not serious.

Tom Politte, a farmer, whose son yesterday shot and wounded the negro, dropped dead today when told of the black's capture. Exhaustion and excitement of the long chase are believed to have caused his death.

POSSE CAPTURES
NEGRO WANTED ON
ASSAULT CHARGE
Vineland, Mo., Aug. 14.—(United Press.)—The negro who attempted to attack 12-year-old Gertrude Wilson of this place last Wednesday and who has since led posses a chase of more than one hundred miles, was found exhausted and wounded twice four miles from the scene of his crime this morning. It was feared he would be lynched.

The negro gave his name as David Robinson of Chicago. He nonchalantly marched along amid the threatening glances of the posse as they started for the city to turn him over to the county authorities.

Tom Pollitte, 65, a farmer, whose son yesterday shot and wounded Robinson, dropped dead today when he was told of the negro's capture. The old man's death is believed to have resulted from the excitement and fatigue of the long chase in which he was an active participant despite his age.
gertrude-wilson-vineland-1920-08-11.A14:
NEGRO FUGITIVE IS CAPTURED AS HE LEAVES COVER Captor Fired Six Shots Before Black Would Surrender.
De Soto, Mo., Aug. 14.—David Robertson, the negro who has confessed his guilt of the attempted attack on Gertrude Wilson, 14-year-old child of a farmer of Blackwell, Mo., was brought to De Soto this afternoon, and placed under a special guard by order of Sheriff Clark. There was no attempt made to gain control of the negro by mob rule, and his arrival in the city, although heralded, failed to create any great excitement.

The negro was captured by Clyde Nickleson, 21 years old, of Richwood, a visitor in this community, who saw the negro as he emerged from an underbrush, and fired six shots at the black, none of them taking effect. The negro surrendered, after Nickleson had fired the shots and begged for his life as his captor backed him to a tree, with an empty revolver.

Reports from various sources during the hunt that the negro had been struck by his pursuers were verified when it was found that he had been shot twice, once in the chest, and a second time in the leg. Neither of the wounds had been treated, and both appeared to be in bad condition.

O. H. White, cashier of the Citizen's Bank of De Soto, announced following the capture of the black, that pictures would be taken of him and his captor, and sold to the citizens, the proceeds from the pictures to be applied to a fund of $170 needed to pay expenses for blood hounds used in searching for the negro.

East St. Louis blood hounds were sent on the trail of the negro last Thursday, but after the trails became old they failed to follow, and they were replaced by other hounds Friday afternoon. No better luck was had with the second set of hounds than with the first, however, and the negro was finally captured only after he slipped from the underbrush alongside a road, and literally gave himself up to the man hunters.
gertrude-wilson-vineland-1920-08-11.A16:
Vineland Man Hunt.
The general hunt for an unknown negro who attempted to assault the 14 year-old daughter of Chas. Wilson, a farmer living near Vineland, last Wednesday morning ended Saturday morning when he was captured in the road within a mile of the scene of his attempted crime by a young man named Clyde Nicholson of Richwoods, who was visiting relatives at Vineland. Young Nicholson, who was alone at the time, had joined the hunt and had a revolver with him. When he saw the negro step out into road from the brush, he emptied the revolver at him, but failed to hit the man. But it caused the fugitive to surrender. He had been chased day and night over the territory of three cornering counties for a hundred miles, until he was so exhausted that he laid down in the road, caring no longer what happened to him as his captor, with revolver reloaded, took him in charge. There was some talk of a necktie party following the capture, but wiser counsel prevailed, and the prisoner was taken to jail at Hillsboro. The excitement of the chase is said to have caused the sudden death of Thos. Politte of Les Mines, at whose place the fugitive appeared Thursday morning and was shot at by one of the Polittes. The negro had been shot twice during his night, but was not seriously wounded

Congressman M. E. Rhodes is now making a canvass of this congressional district and regards the prospects of his re-election by a much larger majority than he had two years ago as very flattering.

Quite a large contingent of Potosians attended the fair at De Sotolast Thursday. They say the fair was good. Most of them made the trip by auto and kept the railroad company out of quite a bunch of coin.

Mr. Elmer Edgar and family of Goodwater were visitors here at the home of County Treasurer N. F. Robinson last week. Elmer said that he was merchandising on his own account at Goodwater and doing quite well.

The work of improvement at Iron Mountain continues and the property is getting in a most presentable condition. Mack Mauzy has three boilers at work pumping the water out of the shaft on the old mountain.—Ironton Register.

Mrs. Florence Dinning, widow of the late Frank Dinning of Potosi, who now makes her home in Jefferson County, has been nominated by the Democratic County Committee for the office of county treasurer of that county.

Rev. W. E. Judy will preach at Shirley next Sunday afternoon at 2:80 o'clock.

Eliza Torrence is having a concrete walk laid in front of his home, filling up a break in the continuity of the walk in that block.

The sale held by J. E. Boques at Old Mines last Saturday was attended by one of the largest sale crowds ever gathered in the county. Everything offered was sold at a good price.

Many autos hereabouts are carrying the "Lift Missouri Out of the Mud" good roads booster device. Our autoist friends should give all the candidates for county judge a careful once over, lest they vote to throw a monkey-wrench in the works.

Our old friend Frank Swacker was in Potosi this week and dropped in to see us. He is just back from a visit of four or five months with relatives in Virginia. He has no permanent home and spends his time between his children in Irondale, Herculaneum and Bridgeton, Mo.

Mr. and Mrs. Thos. Browne of Tiff, good friends of the Journal, were visitors at this office Monday to renew their paper. Mr. Bsown said he was mining tiff on the Bust Bros. land near Tiff and working five days and a half last week he mined ten tons of tiff which brought him six dollar a ton. Sixty dollars for a week's work isn't at all bad.

C. A. Strayer has about completed the improvements on the garage building occupied by the Potosi Motor Sales Co. The front of the building has been altered into a showroom and a large repair shop occupies the rear. The basement is a large storage garage. On the second-ficer are six nice living-rooms, which will be occupied by Ed Hawkins, manager of the business.

David Robinson, the negro who caused a three-days' hunt for him by hundreds of armed men at Vineland a few weeks ago for having attempted to assault a young white girl of the vicinity, has been found insane by the county court of Jefferson County and sent to the state insane asylum at Fulton. During his confinement in jail at Hillsboro the negro is said to have acted like a wild animal.

Some coal is coming in, but the supply is yet far short of the requirements for the winter. Wood, too, is slow in coming in and high in price, yet thousands of cords of good firewood is going to waste in the tie cuttings within easy trucking distance of town. A man with a little enterprise and a truck would be in a fair way of making some money by maintaining a permanent woodyard here.

There was a show in town Monday, Montana Bell's Wild West, and 'twas a motley outfit. One of its most "attractive" features apparently was the girl who ran the doll-rack, who wore khaki britches and puttees, military style, and she wasn't a bad looker at that. The menagerie consisted of a wolf and some kind of a wild bird. There were some other "birds" in the company. We did not witness the performance, Belle being stingy with the combs, but from all we can learn of the performance, we did not miss much.
